name: Waterfall Approach
definition: A development approach that completes each stage (requirements, design, development, testing, installation, maintenance) in order, with each stage signed off before the next begins.
example: A council system built to a signed specification, with testing only after all development is finished.

name: Agile Approach
definition: A development approach that builds a system in short cycles, with a working piece and client feedback at the end of each cycle.
example: A club booking app delivered in two-week sprints, with the club secretary reviewing each one.

name: Sprint
definition: A short, fixed-length work cycle in Scrum, typically one to four weeks, that ends in a working increment and a review.
example: A two-week sprint to build the login and timetable screens.

name: Product Backlog
definition: A prioritised list of the features and tasks still to be done in an agile project.
example: A list with 'online payment' at the top and 'loyalty points' near the bottom.

name: End-User Development
definition: A development approach in which the people who will use a system build or adapt it themselves with accessible tools such as spreadsheets.
example: A bookkeeper building a stock tracker in a spreadsheet for her own use.

name: Outsourcing
definition: Paying another organisation, possibly in another country, to build or run part or all of a system.
example: A start-up paying a software company to build its payment feature.

name: Critical Path
definition: The longest chain of dependent tasks in a project plan, which decides the earliest finish date; a delay to any task on it delays the project.
example: Interview, design screens, build and test add up to 16 days, so any delay to them delays handover.

name: Float (Slack)
definition: The number of days a task can be delayed without delaying the end date of the project.
example: Designing the database has 2 days of float because the build cannot start until the screens are designed.

name: Milestone
definition: A significant point in a project, such as an approval or delivery, marked on a Gantt chart as a point in time rather than a task with duration.
example: 'Requirements approved' on 23 October.

name: MoSCoW Prioritisation
definition: A common technique that sorts requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time).
example: Ordering canteen app features so online ordering is a Must and loyalty points a Could.

name: Feasibility Check
definition: An assessment of whether a project can be delivered, commonly looking at technical, economic, schedule and operational feasibility.
example: Deciding that an online payment feature is not feasible with no budget and no skills.

name: Risk Register
definition: A table listing possible project risks with their likelihood, consequence, response and owner.
example: A row for 'client unavailable for two weeks' with a plan to book meetings in advance.

name: Contingency
definition: Time or money set aside to cover problems that cannot be predicted.
example: Adding a 10% reserve to a project budget.

name: Boundary Test Data
definition: Test values at the edge of the allowed range and just either side of it.
example: For a quantity of 1 to 20: 0, 1, 20 and 21.

name: Erroneous Test Data
definition: Test data that should be rejected because it is the wrong type, is missing or is impossible.
example: Entering 'abc', a blank or 2.5 into a whole-number quantity field.

name: Version History
definition: A record kept by a file or collaboration tool of who changed a file and when, allowing earlier versions to be restored.
example: Restoring yesterday's version of a shared design document.

name: Success Criteria
definition: Measurable statements, set at the start of a project, that describe what a solution must achieve to be judged successful.
example: Staff can enter an order in under one minute.

name: Scope Creep
definition: The uncontrolled growth of a project's requirements after they were agreed.
example: A client adds three new features after sign-off without any change to the deadline.

name: Stakeholder
definition: A person or group who is involved in, or affected by, a project or the system it produces.
example: The canteen manager, students who order, and parents who pay.

name: Action Plan
definition: A short-range list of tasks with an owner, a due date and a status, usually drawn from a Gantt chart.
example: A weekly table of who builds the Menu tables and by which day.

name: Implementation Plan
definition: A plan for how a new system goes live, including the changeover method, steps and dates, training, risks and a fallback.
example: A pilot in one depot, then rollout to four others, with the old system kept for a fortnight.

name: Deliverable
definition: A specific item that a project must produce and hand over, such as a working system, a user guide or a test report.
example: The user guide handed to the canteen manager.

name: System Maintenance
definition: Work done after a system goes live to fix faults, adapt it to changes and improve it.
example: Updating a booking system when the club adds a new membership type.
